title: Real-time: polling, SSE, WebSockets, push
scopeHtml: Scope: short and long polling, SSE, WebSockets, connection scaling, heartbeats and reconnect, push notifications, choosing a technique.

notes.title: The real-time problem
notes.html:
HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers, and the server cannot speak first. But chat messages, live scores, driver locations and notifications are things the server knows first. Real-time techniques are different tricks to get new data to the client quickly.

Five options, from simplest to most capable:

  1. Short polling: ask every few seconds.
  2. Long polling: ask, and the server holds the request open until it has news.
  3. Server-Sent Events (SSE): one long HTTP response that streams events down.
  4. WebSockets: a full two-way connection after an HTTP upgrade.
  5. Push notifications (FCM/APNs): the OS wakes your app even when it is closed.

Worked example. 1M users, "is there a new message?" Polling every 5 s = 200,000 requests/s, of which 95%+ return "nothing new". Push over a held connection needs no repeated asking: you pay in open connections, not request rate.

Industry examples. WhatsApp (persistent connection over its own XMPP-derived protocol), Slack (WebSocket), Zerodha Kite (WebSocket for ticks), Gmail web (long polling then other channels), Twitter/X live feed (SSE-style streaming), Uber (push + persistent connections).

Everyday analogy. Checking the letterbox every minute (polling), waiting at the post office counter until a parcel arrives (long polling), a phone call (WebSocket), a doorbell that rings in your pocket even while you sleep (push).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to WebSockets without asking if the data truly needs two-way, low-latency flow.
  • Not putting a number on how many open connections it means.

notes.title: Short polling
notes.html:
The client calls GET /status on a timer (every N seconds) and the server replies immediately, with data or "nothing".

Pros: dead simple, works through every proxy, firewall and CDN, stateless servers, easy to cache and rate limit. Cons: wasted requests; latency up to the interval (average N/2); battery drain on mobile (waking the radio every 5 s keeps it in a high-power state); server load grows with users times frequency.

Improvements: use If-None-Match/ETag so empty polls are cheap 304s; adaptive intervals (poll fast only while the user is on the screen, back off when idle); jitter so 1M clients do not poll in the same second.

Worked example. Order-tracking page, 200,000 active orders, poll every 10 s = 20,000 req/s. At about 1 KB per response with headers, 20 MB/s. Acceptable for a short-lived screen; wasteful if the data changes once every 5 minutes.

When it is right. Job status (GET /jobs/77 until done), dashboards updating every 30 to 60 s, anything where seconds of delay are fine and simplicity wins.

Industry examples. Early Twitter, many async-job APIs (Google long-running operations, payment status pages), CI dashboards.

Everyday analogy. A child in the car asking "are we there yet?" every minute.

Common interview traps.

  • Fixed interval for all clients, causing synchronized spikes after a deploy or outage.
  • Ignoring mobile battery cost.

notes.title: Long polling
notes.html:
Long polling is polling where the server delays its reply until there is data (or a timeout, say 30 to 60 s), then the client immediately reconnects.

Mechanism: client sends last_event_id; the server checks for newer events; if none, parks the request (non-blocking, e.g. Netty/Node/async servlet) and completes it when something is published or the timeout fires. The client then re-issues the request at once. Using the last-seen id means that events occurring during the reconnect gap are not lost.

Pros: near real-time over plain HTTP, works everywhere (including old proxies), no special protocol, tolerates restarts. Cons: a held request per client (threads must not block: use async IO), a full HTTP request/response overhead per event, ordering and duplicate care, proxies/load balancers may cut idle connections (set their idle timeout above your hold time, e.g. hold 25 s with a 60 s LB timeout), and bursts of events cause rapid reconnect loops.

Android sketch:

suspend fun longPoll(api: Api) {
    var lastId = store.lastId()
    while (currentCoroutineContext().isActive) {
        try {
            val resp = api.events(lastId, timeoutSec = 25)   // server holds up to 25s
            resp.events.forEach { handle(it); lastId = it.id }
            store.saveLastId(lastId)
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            delay(backoffWithJitter())                         // network drop
        }
    }
}

Worked example. 100,000 connected clients with a 25 s hold: about 4,000 reconnect requests/s when idle. Versus short polling every 2 s (for similar freshness) at 50,000 req/s. Event delay drops from up to 2 s to a few ms.

Industry examples. Facebook Messenger (early web chat), Gmail's older chat, the Comet pattern, Telegram getUpdates with timeout, Slack's legacy RTM fallback.

Everyday analogy. Standing at the post office window saying "I will wait here until my parcel arrives", then going back to queue again the moment you receive one.

Common interview traps.

  • Blocking one thread per held request; 10k clients need 10k threads.
  • Missing events between reconnects (no last-id/cursor).
  • Proxy idle timeout shorter than the hold time, producing errors at fixed intervals.

notes.title: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
notes.html:
SSE is a single long-lived HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream where the server keeps writing small text messages; the client auto-reconnects. One direction only: server to client.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

id: 121
event: price
data: {"symbol":"INFY","ltp":1543.2}

: heartbeat comment

id: 122
data: {"symbol":"TCS","ltp":4120.5}

Details:

  • Browser EventSource handles parsing and automatic reconnection; on reconnect it sends Last-Event-ID: 122 so the server can resume. Server may set retry: 3000 (ms).
  • Plain text, UTF-8 only (binary needs base64).
  • Uses ordinary HTTP, so it passes proxies, auth headers (mostly), HTTP/2 multiplexing (many streams on one connection; on HTTP/1.1 browsers cap about 6 connections per domain, a classic SSE gotcha).
  • Beware proxy buffering: NGINX needs proxy_buffering off; and X-Accel-Buffering: no, or events arrive in clumps.
  • On Android use OkHttp's okhttp-sse (EventSources) rather than EventSource (browser only).

Worked example. Live cricket score, 2M viewers, one update per 3 s of about 200 bytes. Per client: 67 B/s. Total egress: 2M x 67 B/s = 134 MB/s ≈ 1.07 Gbps. Fan-out is the real cost: use a pub-sub (Redis/Kafka) feeding many edge nodes, or a CDN with SSE support, and push the same bytes to many connections. Open connections: 2M; at about 50 KB/connection that is 100 GB of RAM across nodes (say 20 nodes of 100k connections).

Pros. Simple, text, standard HTTP, built-in reconnect and resume, great for feeds, notifications, progress bars, LLM token streaming (ChatGPT/Claude APIs stream with SSE). Cons. One-way, no binary, connection limit on HTTP/1.1, some corporate proxies buffer.

Industry examples. OpenAI and Anthropic streaming APIs, Mastodon streaming, GitHub-like live logs, Heroku logs, Twitter/X filtered stream (chunked JSON).

Everyday analogy. A radio broadcast: you tune in and it talks to you; you cannot talk back on the same channel.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing WebSockets when SSE is enough (a simpler, more proxy-friendly answer is a plus).
  • Forgetting buffering settings and HTTP/1.1 connection limits.
  • No event ids, so reconnects drop events.

notes.title: WebSockets
notes.html:
A WebSocket is a persistent, full-duplex (both directions at once) TCP connection that starts as an HTTP request and is "upgraded".

Handshake:

GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

After 101, both sides send frames (text or binary, 2 to 14 bytes header overhead vs hundreds of bytes for HTTP headers). Control frames: ping, pong, close.

Pros: lowest latency, tiny per-message overhead, binary support, server and client both can push (chat, games, collaborative editing, trading). Cons: stateful connections (hard to scale and deploy), no built-in reconnect or message replay (you build it), no HTTP caching, some proxies/firewalls interfere (use wss:// on 443 to pass), authentication only at handshake (send a token in the first message or a short-lived ticket in the URL query; headers are not settable from browser WebSocket API), and load balancers must support upgrade and long idle timeouts.

Android (OkHttp):

val ws = client.newWebSocket(
    Request.Builder().url("wss://api.example.com/chat").build(),
    object : WebSocketListener() {
        override fun onMessage(ws: WebSocket, text: String) { handle(text) }
        override fun onFailure(ws: WebSocket, t: Throwable, r: Response?) { scheduleReconnect() }
    })
ws.send("""{"type":"send","to":"u2","text":"hi","client_msg_id":"c-77"}""")

Worked example. Chat with 5M concurrent users, each sends about 1 message/min of 300 bytes: 83k msgs/s inbound. Per-connection memory about 20 to 50 KB (kernel buffers + app objects) so 5M connections ≈ 100 to 250 GB of RAM, around 50 to 100 gateway nodes of 100k connections each (WhatsApp famously reached 1M+ connections per Erlang server around 2012).

Industry examples. Slack, Discord (gateway over WebSocket with heartbeat and resume), Zerodha/Upstox market data, Figma and Google Docs collaboration, Phoenix Channels, Socket.IO (adds fallbacks and rooms).

Everyday analogy. A phone call: once connected, either side can talk at any moment, but someone must keep the line open.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying WebSockets are "just faster HTTP". They are a different, stateful model.
  • Not designing for reconnect, replay and duplicates.
  • Putting the auth token in the URL without making it short-lived (it lands in logs).

notes.title: Scaling connections
notes.html:
The unit of scale for real-time is the number of concurrent open connections, not requests per second.

What limits one machine:

  • File descriptors: each connection is one; raise ulimit -n (e.g. 1,000,000) and fs.file-max.
  • Memory: about 10 to 50 KB per connection; 1M connections ≈ 10 to 50 GB.
  • Ephemeral ports only matter on the client/proxy side (65k per source IP to one destination). A load balancer to backend hop can exhaust them: use multiple IPs or ports.
  • CPU for TLS handshakes during reconnect storms (a mass reconnect after a deploy is the main danger).
  • Event loop design: epoll/kqueue with async IO (Netty, Node, Go, Erlang), not thread per connection. 100k to 1M connections per box is feasible with tuning.

Sysctl/config style:

# Linux
sysctl -w fs.file-max=2000000
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65535
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="1024 65535"
ulimit -n 1000000

Architecture: stateless gateway layer + pub/sub. A user's connection is on gateway node G7, but the sender's message is handled on G2. You need a way to route to the right node:

  • A presence/routing store (Redis hash: user:42 -> gateway-7) records where each user is connected (with TTL refreshed by heartbeats).
  • Sender's service looks up the node and publishes to that node's channel (Redis Pub/Sub, NATS, or a Kafka topic partitioned by user).
  • Or broadcast by room: all gateways subscribe to the room channel and forward to local sockets.
  • Fan-out to big groups (a 100,000-member channel) uses a write-once, many-readers approach: publish once, each gateway fans out locally.

Load balancing:

  • L4 or L7 balancer with long idle timeouts (AWS ALB supports WebSockets; set idle timeout above your heartbeat interval, e.g. 120 s vs 30 s ping; NGINX proxy_read_timeout 3600s).
  • Least-connections instead of round robin (long-lived connections get uneven).
  • Draining on deploy: tell the gateway to stop accepting, send a "reconnect later" signal with jitter, and rate-limit reconnects to avoid a thundering herd.
  • Sticky routing is not needed if state lives in Redis; it is only needed per connection, which the TCP connection already provides.

Worked example. 10M concurrent connections, 100k per node = 100 nodes plus 30% headroom = 130 nodes. A deploy rolling 10% at a time reconnects 1M clients over, say, 60 s = 16,700 reconnects/s, each doing a TLS handshake and an auth check. Cap with server-side connection rate limits and client random delay of 0 to 30 s.

Incident pattern. After a gateway crash, all its 100k clients reconnect simultaneously to the remaining nodes; CPU saturates on TLS, auth DB gets slammed, and the cascade spreads. Metrics: connection count sawtooth, handshake rate spike, p99 connect latency, auth DB QPS. Defences: jittered backoff, admission control, session resumption tickets, auth tokens validated locally (JWT) rather than by DB.

Industry examples. WhatsApp (Erlang, about 1M+ connections per server in its early scaling posts), Discord (Elixir gateway with sessions that can resume), Slack (WebSocket gateway servers by region), Pusher/Ably as managed services, Twitch chat (IRC-based edge nodes).

Everyday analogy. A switchboard operator: the hard part is not the volume of words but how many lines are plugged in at once and knowing which plug is which person.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing capacity from requests per second and ignoring concurrent connections and memory.
  • No routing layer: how does server A reach a user connected to server B?
  • Round-robin LB with WebSockets, then rolling deploys leave nodes unbalanced.
  • Forgetting reconnect storms.

notes.title: Heartbeats and reconnect
notes.html:
A connection can die silently: phone enters a tunnel, NAT drops the mapping, Wi-Fi switches to 4G. TCP may not notice for minutes. Heartbeats detect dead connections; reconnect logic restores them.

Heartbeat (ping/pong):

  • Either side sends a ping every 20 to 30 s; expects pong within about 10 s; no pong means the connection is dead, so close it and reconnect.
  • It also keeps NATs and load balancers from dropping an "idle" connection (mobile carrier NATs often time out in 30 to 60 s for idle TCP; some LBs at 60 s; set your interval below the shortest).
  • Server side: evict connections that miss 2 to 3 heartbeats; update the presence TTL (for example presence key TTL 60 s refreshed every 25 s).
  • WebSocket protocol has ping/pong control frames; OkHttp: OkHttpClient.Builder().pingInterval(25, TimeUnit.SECONDS). Also an app-level heartbeat helps because proxies may answer protocol pings on your behalf.
  • SSE: server sends a comment line (: keepalive) every 15 to 25 s.
  • Battery trade-off on mobile: very frequent heartbeats drain battery; a 25 to 30 s interval is common while foregrounded, and apps drop the socket when backgrounded and rely on push.

Reconnect:

  1. Exponential backoff with jitter: wait random(0, min(30 s, 1 s * 2^attempt)); reset after a stable connection (say 60 s).
  2. Resume, not restart: send the last received sequence number or event id; the server replays missed messages from a short buffer (Discord "resume", SSE Last-Event-ID). If the gap is too large, the client does a full resync via REST.
  3. Idempotent delivery: server assigns message ids; clients dedupe; clients send client_msg_id so retried sends are not doubled.
  4. Network awareness: on Android use ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback to reconnect immediately when a network returns instead of waiting for the timer; stop trying when offline.
  5. Authentication on reconnect: refresh the access token first; a stale token would loop forever on 401.
fun backoffMs(attempt: Int): Long {
    val cap = 30_000L
    val exp = minOf(cap, 1_000L shl minOf(attempt, 5))
    return (0..exp).random()          // full jitter
}

Worked example. 1M clients, drop of a gateway at the same time. Without jitter all retry after exactly 1 s, 2 s, 4 s: 1M connects in the same second. With full jitter over a 0 to 8 s window, about 125k/s on average, which a fleet can absorb with admission limits.

Industry examples. Discord's gateway protocol (heartbeat interval sent by the server, sequence numbers, resume), Socket.IO ping interval/timeout defaults (check version docs), MQTT keep-alive (used by Facebook Messenger on mobile and many IoT systems), AWS IoT.

Everyday analogy. On a phone call you say "hello, still there?" after a long silence; if no answer, you hang up, call back, and say "where were we? I last heard...".

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on TCP to report a dead peer.
  • Retrying at a fixed interval with no jitter.
  • Reconnecting but not resuming, so messages are lost; or resuming without dedupe, so messages duplicate.

notes.title: Push notifications
notes.html:
Push notifications deliver a small message to a device even when the app is closed, through the OS vendor's persistent connection: FCM (Firebase Cloud Messaging) on Android, APNs on iOS.

Why the vendor channel? Android keeps one shared connection from the OS (Google Play Services) to FCM for all apps. That is far cheaper for battery than every app holding its own socket, and it can wake a killed app. Your backend never connects to the phone directly.

Flow:

  1. App gets a registration token from FCM (FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().token) and sends it to your backend with the user id. Tokens rotate; handle onNewToken.
  2. Backend sends a request to FCM HTTP v1 API (POST https://fcm.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<id>/messages:send) with the token and payload.
  3. FCM delivers to the device (store-and-forward if offline, up to the TTL).
  4. App shows the notification or handles a data message in FirebaseMessagingService.onMessageReceived.

Message types:

  • Notification message: FCM/system shows it when the app is in background; the app code runs only on tap (when in foreground, callback runs).
  • Data message: delivered to your code, you decide what to do; used to trigger a sync.
  • Priority: high can wake the device immediately (limited by Doze and app standby buckets; abuse gets demoted), normal is batched. ttl sets how long FCM retains it (up to 4 weeks); collapse_key replaces older pending messages (only the latest "new messages" signal matters).
  • Payload limit: about 4 KB. Do not put secrets or big content in it; send a hint and fetch details over HTTPS.

Delivery is best effort: not guaranteed, not ordered, can be delayed in Doze, dropped for force-stopped apps or when the user disables notifications. So design: push = wake-up signal, REST sync = source of truth, and for chat also keep the socket when the app is in the foreground.

Typical mixed design:

  • App in foreground: WebSocket/SSE for live updates.
  • App in background/killed: FCM data message, which triggers a short sync (WorkManager or expedited work).
  • Notification shown with deduplication via notification id so a socket message and a push for the same event do not both alert.

Scaling the sender: a campaign to 10M devices. FCM allows up to a set rate per project (check docs, historically in the order of hundreds of thousands per minute with default quotas, and topic/batch sends); queue the sends (Kafka/SQS), run N worker processes, handle UNREGISTERED/NOT_FOUND tokens by deleting them, and honor 429/503 with Retry-After and backoff. Use topics for broadcasts ("sports-score-india") so you do not iterate tokens yourself.

Worked example. 10M-user news app, breaking alert: 10M sends. With 50 workers each doing 2,000 sends/s = 100k/s → 100 s to complete. 8% of tokens are stale; they return unregistered and are purged, shrinking future sends.

Industry examples. WhatsApp and Telegram use a push to wake the app then fetch the message over their own connection; Uber and Swiggy order updates use FCM plus in-app socket/polling; Gmail uses push to trigger sync; Zomato/Swiggy marketing pushes use segmented batches.

Everyday analogy. A courier who knocks on your door with a note "you have a package at the depot": the note is small and unreliable, the depot is where the real parcel is.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating push as reliable delivery (no fallback sync).
  • Sending sensitive data in the payload.
  • Never cleaning invalid tokens; costs and error rates grow.
  • Ignoring Doze/battery restrictions and OEM background kills (Xiaomi, Oppo).

notes.title: Choosing the technique
notes.html:
Pick the simplest technique that meets the latency and direction requirements.

Need Pick Why
Job done? Every 5 to 60 s freshness is fine Short polling Simplest, cacheable
Near real-time, restrictive network, low event rate Long polling Works over plain HTTP
Server → client stream (feeds, scores, LLM tokens) SSE Simple, auto-reconnect, HTTP-friendly
Two-way, low latency (chat, games, collaboration, trading) WebSocket Full duplex, small frames
App closed or backgrounded Push (FCM/APNs) Only way to wake the app
Huge fan-out, IoT, flaky networks MQTT Built-in QoS, small footprint

Cost comparison for 1M users that each need updates within 2 s:

  • Short poll at 2 s: 500k req/s, almost all empty.
  • Long poll: 1M parked requests, a few thousand reconnects/s, event-driven.
  • SSE/WebSocket: 1M connections; tiny steady cost, but memory and connection management.

Decision gravity. Moving from polling to WebSocket later is a client + gateway change but the REST fallback remains, so it is a two-way door if you keep the REST sync path as the source of truth. The one-way part is the message id/ordering model: define sequence numbers and idempotent delivery from day one.

Industry examples. Slack: WebSocket + REST backfill + push; WhatsApp: persistent connection + push; Gmail: push + sync; ChatGPT: SSE streaming; Zerodha: WebSocket binary ticks.

Everyday analogy. Use a notice board for slow news, a loudspeaker for broadcasts, a phone call for conversations, and a doorbell for when you are asleep.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking one mechanism for all states of the app (foreground vs background).
  • Forgetting a REST catch-up path after a long disconnect.
  • Not stating the failure story: what the user sees when the socket is down.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Real-time = getting server-known data to the client fast. Options: short polling, long polling, SSE, WebSockets, push.
  • Short polling: simple but wasteful; add ETag, adaptive intervals and jitter. Long polling: held request, reconnect with last id, use async IO and watch proxy timeouts.
  • SSE: one-way text stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID, turn off proxy buffering. WebSocket: full-duplex after a 101 upgrade; you must build auth, reconnect and replay.
  • Scaling = concurrent connections: file descriptors, 10 to 50 KB each, epoll-based servers, a gateway layer with a presence store plus pub/sub, least-connections balancing, long idle timeouts, jittered reconnects and draining on deploys.
  • Heartbeats (ping every 20 to 30 s, shorter than NAT/LB timeouts) detect dead links; reconnect with exponential backoff plus full jitter, resume from a sequence number, dedupe with message ids.
  • Push (FCM/APNs): best-effort wake-up signal, small payload, collapse keys and TTL, clean up invalid tokens, REST sync stays the source of truth.
  • Combine: socket in the foreground, push in the background, REST for catch-up.

questions.promptHtml: HTTP is request-response. How do you get server-side events to a client quickly? Compare the options.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Opening question for chat, feed and live-score designs; checks if you reason from direction and latency, not from the buzzword WebSocket.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The server cannot speak first in plain HTTP, so there are five tricks. Short polling asks every few seconds. Long polling asks and the server holds the request until there is news. SSE is one long HTTP response streaming events one way. WebSocket is a two-way connection after an HTTP upgrade. Push (FCM/APNs) wakes the app when it is closed. I pick the simplest one that meets the latency and direction I need.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think in cost: polling costs requests per second, the others cost open connections.

  • 1M users polling every 5 s = 200,000 req/s, 95% returning "nothing new".
  • Held connections need no repeated asking, but each costs 10 to 50 KB of memory, so 1M connections is 10 to 50 GB.
Short poll : client asks every N s            (latency up to N, avg N/2)
Long poll  : client asks, server parks it     (latency ~ms, 1 request per event)
SSE        : server streams text events       (one way, auto-reconnect)
WebSocket  : full duplex frames               (two way, you build reconnect)
Push       : OS channel wakes the app         (best effort, tiny payload)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Jumping to WebSockets without asking if data is two-way.
  • No number for how many open connections that means.
  • One technique for all app states; background needs push.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Direction is server to client only. -> SSE, simpler and proxy friendly.
  2. App is killed. -> Push wake-up, then REST sync.
  3. Why is the REST path still needed? -> Source of truth after any gap; push and sockets are best effort.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "WebSockets for real-time". Senior: states direction, latency target and connection count, combines socket in foreground, push in background, REST for catch-up.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used WebSockets for a one-way price ticker and spent a quarter building reconnect and replay that SSE gives for free.

questions.promptHtml: How does Server-Sent Events work, and what are its limits compared to WebSockets?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: SSE is underused; knowing it, plus its gotchas, signals practical experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SSE is one long HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream where the server writes small text events. The client auto-reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. It is one-way, text only, and works through ordinary HTTP infrastructure. Limits: no binary, no client-to-server channel on the same stream, a six-connection cap per domain on HTTP/1.1 browsers, and proxy buffering that can clump events.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

id: 121
event: price
data: {"symbol":"INFY","ltp":1543.2}

: heartbeat comment

Details: retry: 3000 sets reconnect delay; a comment line (: keepalive) every 15 to 25 s keeps proxies from closing the stream; browsers use EventSource, Android uses okhttp-sse. Behind NGINX set proxy_buffering off and X-Accel-Buffering: no. On HTTP/2 many streams share one connection, removing the six-connection issue.

Cost example: 2M viewers, one 200-byte event per 3 s = 67 B/s each, 134 MB/s (about 1 Gbps) total egress; fan-out via pub-sub to edge nodes, about 100k connections per node.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing WebSocket when SSE is enough.
  • No event ids, so reconnect drops events.
  • Forgetting buffering and the HTTP/1.1 connection limit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you send data client to server? -> Normal HTTP POST alongside the stream.
  2. Auth? -> Cookies or tokens in headers (native clients); browser EventSource cannot set headers, so use cookies or a short-lived ticket.
  3. LLM token streaming? -> Same mechanism; each token chunk is an event.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "one-way WebSocket". Senior: resume with ids, buffering, HTTP/2 multiplexing, fan-out cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Live logs arrived every 30 seconds in bursts until proxy_buffering off was set on the ingress.

questions.contextHtml:
A job-progress page uses SSE. Works on localhost. In production, progress jumps 0% to 100% after 40 s instead of updating each second; and every ~60 s the console shows a reconnect. Setup: browser -> ALB (idle timeout 60 s) -> NGINX -> app. NGINX config:

location /events {
    proxy_pass http://app;
}

App response headers: Content-Type: text/event-stream. App emits an event every 1 s and nothing else.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "SSE is unreliable, switch to WebSockets." The mechanism is the same TCP path; the config is wrong.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is gzip on? Is there a CDN? Are events flushed in the app (flush after each write)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the proxy settings and a heartbeat.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: NGINX buffers the response by default so events arrive in clumps; ALB idle 60 s closes quiet streams; app does not flush; gzip buffers.
  4. How I'd verify: curl -N https://host/events and watch if events trickle; compare with a direct curl to the app.
  5. Root cause: proxy_buffering on (default) holds data until a buffer fills or the response ends. The 60 s reconnect is the ALB idle timeout, with no events between bursts.
  6. Fix:
location /events {
    proxy_pass http://app;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
    add_header X-Accel-Buffering no;
}

App: flush after each event, send : keepalive every 15 s (below the 60 s ALB timeout), put id: on events so reconnect resumes. 7. Prevention: An integration test that goes through the real ingress; synthetic probe measuring event spacing. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise the LB timeout to hours as the only fix; heartbeats also detect dead clients.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 50k viewers on one page and HTTP/1.1? -> Browsers cap about 6 connections per domain; use HTTP/2.
  • Client reconnects and misses events? -> Send Last-Event-ID handling on the server with a short replay buffer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dashboard looked "laggy" for months; the cause was a default buffering setting in an ingress controller.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Switch protocol.
  • Hire: Buffering off, heartbeat under LB timeout.
  • Strong hire: Also flush, ids, HTTP/2 and an end-to-end test.

questions.contextHtml: Order-tracking screen of a food app: 200,000 concurrent active orders, the Android client polls GET /orders/{id}/status every 3 s. Status changes about 6 times per order over 40 minutes. Backend: 6,700 req/s at 12% CPU but the DB read replica is at 60%. Users complain the app drains battery. Product wants "live" updates but with no big rewrite this quarter.
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut cost and battery without moving to WebSockets?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Poll less often." That makes tracking stale and ignores why most polls are wasted.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What latency is acceptable per state (driver location vs "delivered")? Is the screen always foreground? Is there a CDN or cache layer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return ETag and 304 Not Modified; cache status in Redis for 1 to 2 s instead of hitting the replica.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 99% of polls return unchanged data (6 changes per 800 polls); the radio wake every 3 s drains battery; synchronized intervals create spikes after deploys.
  4. How I'd verify: Ratio of 304 or identical bodies, replica QPS, a battery profile on a test device.
  5. Root cause: Fixed fast interval for slow-changing data.
  6. Fix: Adaptive interval: 3 s while an event is imminent (driver arriving), 15 to 30 s otherwise, stop when the screen is off; jitter ±20%; server hint next_poll_after in the response; push (FCM) for state changes as the primary signal with polling as fallback. Math: from 6,700 to roughly 1,300 req/s at 15 s average.
  7. Prevention: Metric of "useful poll ratio" and a per-endpoint polling budget.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not poll faster to feel real-time. Long polling or SSE is the next step if freshness under 2 s is needed; the REST status endpoint remains the source of truth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rider location every 2 s on a map? -> Now streaming fits; SSE or WebSocket scoped to the active-order screen.
  • App backgrounded? -> Stop polling and rely on push.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Server-hinted poll intervals let one team cut 70% of load during an incident by changing a single config value, without a client release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Poll less often.
  • Hire: ETag, adaptive interval, push for changes.
  • Strong hire: Server hints, jitter, math, and the path to SSE.

questions.contextHtml:
Support chat widget uses long polling: GET /poll?timeout=60. Since a load balancer change on Monday, users report "messages arrive late or not at all". Metrics:

LB idle timeout: 60 s (was 120 s)
poll responses 504 every 60.0 s: 4,100/min
server held requests: 52,000 ; app threads blocked: 52,000/200 pool
messages table: rows with delivered=false age > 5 min: growing

The client re-issues /poll immediately on any response and does not send any cursor.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is wrong and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the thread pool to 60,000."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the server async or thread-per-request? How does the client know what it has seen? What happens to events published during the reconnect gap?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore the LB idle timeout to 120 s and lower the hold time to 25 s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hold time equals the LB timeout so the LB races the server; no last_id cursor, so events during the gap are lost; blocking threads limit capacity.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare time-to-504 against LB timeout; test publishing during a reconnect window; thread dump.
  5. Root cause: Hold time 60 s equals idle timeout 60 s: the LB cuts first. Without a cursor, the events between disconnect and the next request are never replayed.
  6. Fix: Hold 25 s with LB timeout 60 s; client sends last_event_id; server returns all events after that id immediately if any exist, else parks; use async IO (Netty or an async servlet) so held requests do not hold threads. Android sketch:
var lastId = store.lastId()
while (isActive) {
    try {
        val r = api.events(lastId, timeoutSec = 25)
        r.events.forEach { handle(it); lastId = it.id }
        store.saveLastId(lastId)
    } catch (e: IOException) { delay(backoffWithJitter()) }
}
  1. Prevention: Test with a proxy that kills idle connections; alert on 504 at fixed intervals.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a bigger pool. If event rates grow, move to SSE or WebSocket; long polling costs a full HTTP request per event.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 100k clients idle at 25 s hold? -> About 4,000 reconnects/s.
  • Dupes after retry? -> Dedupe by event id on the client.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Errors appearing at exact multiples of a timeout almost always mean two layers with equal timeouts.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Bigger thread pool.
  • Hire: Hold shorter than LB, cursor.
  • Strong hire: Async IO, dedupe, exact-interval diagnosis.

questions.contextHtml: A chat app has 500k concurrent WebSocket connections on 10 gateway nodes (50k each, 16 GB RAM, 8 cores). Marketing plans a launch for 5M concurrent. Each user sends about 1 message per minute of 300 bytes. Node metrics at 50k connections: memory 3 GB, CPU 12%, file descriptors 51k of 65k limit. A teammate says "scale linearly: 100 nodes".
questions.promptHtml: Size the fleet, name the limits you will hit first, and describe the routing layer.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "100 nodes, done." Ignores fd limits, deploy storms and cross-node routing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak vs average concurrency? Group chat sizes? Presence required? Acceptable reconnect time after a node loss?
  2. Immediate mitigation (before the launch): Raise fd limits (ulimit -n 1000000, fs.file-max), tune somaxconn.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (limits): (a) fd limit hit first at 65k, (b) memory about 60 KB per connection here, (c) TLS handshake CPU during reconnect, (d) pub-sub fan-out and presence store load.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test with a connection simulator ramping to 200k per node; watch ss -s, RSS per connection, GC.
  5. Root cause of risk: Capacity is concurrent connections, not request rate: inbound is 5M/60 = 83k msgs/s, trivial; the cost is holding 5M sockets.
  6. Fix (design): Per node 100k connections = 50 nodes, plus 30% headroom = 65 nodes. Stateless services behind the gateways. Presence store (Redis hash user:42 -> gateway-7 with TTL refreshed by heartbeats). Sender service looks up the node and publishes to that node's channel (NATS, Redis pub-sub or Kafka partitioned by user). Least-connections load balancing, idle timeout above heartbeat (120 s vs 30 s ping).
Phone A -> GW2 -> pub-sub -> GW7 -> Phone B
                  GW7 -> presence store (TTL)
  1. Prevention: Per-node connection ceilings, canary at 10% traffic, and a capacity dashboard.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not run 5M on 5 giant nodes (blast radius: losing one reconnects 1M clients). Not round robin (long-lived connections skew).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A 100k member group? -> Publish once to a room channel; each gateway fans out to local sockets.
  • Deploys? -> Drain nodes with jittered "reconnect later" and cap reconnect rate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Memory per connection doubled after a library upgrade changed buffer sizes; the capacity model was off by 2x until the load test caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Linear scaling, no routing.
  • Hire: Computes connections and memory, presence plus pub-sub.
  • Strong hire: Blast radius, fd and TLS limits, drain strategy, load test.

questions.subtopic: WebSocket handshake and what you must build
questions.promptHtml: How does a WebSocket connection start, and what does the protocol not give you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who have operated WebSockets from those who say "it is faster HTTP".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It starts as an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket; the server replies 101 Switching Protocols, and from then on both sides send small frames in either direction over the same TCP connection. The protocol gives full duplex and low overhead (2 to 14 bytes per frame). It does not give reconnect, message replay, ordering across reconnects, auth beyond the handshake, or caching; I build those myself.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

Frames: text, binary, ping, pong, close. Browser WebSocket API cannot set headers, so auth uses a cookie or a short-lived ticket in the query string (kept short because URLs land in logs). Use wss:// on 443 to pass middleboxes. Load balancers need upgrade support and long idle timeouts. The server is stateful: each connection lives on one node, so a routing layer is needed (see scaling).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating it as stateless HTTP.
  • Long-lived JWT in the URL.
  • No client message id, so retries after reconnect duplicate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you authenticate? -> Ticket from an authenticated REST call, validated at handshake; re-validate periodically.
  2. When SSE instead? -> One-way streams.
  3. Why ping/pong at app level too? -> Proxies may answer protocol pings on behalf of a dead client.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "persistent two-way connection". Senior: lists what is missing (resume, ordering, dedupe, backpressure) and how deploys and LBs interact.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team put a 24-hour JWT in the WebSocket URL and later found it in CDN logs.

questions.promptHtml: How do you detect a dead connection and reconnect without losing or duplicating messages?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Mobile networks silently die; this tests protocol design, not API knowledge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TCP may not notice a dead peer for minutes, so I send a ping every 20 to 30 s and treat a missing pong within about 10 s as dead; the interval stays below the shortest NAT or LB idle timeout. On reconnect I use exponential backoff with full jitter, then resume by sending the last sequence number so the server replays what I missed; if the gap is too large I do a full REST resync. Messages carry server ids and client send ids so duplicates are dropped.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Server evicts connections missing 2 to 3 heartbeats and refreshes the presence TTL (for example key TTL 60 s refreshed every 25 s).
  • Backoff: random(0, min(30s, 1s * 2^attempt)), reset after about 60 s stable.
  • Reconnect triggers: Android ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback, refresh the token first or a 401 loops forever.
  • With 1M clients dropping together, no jitter means 1M connects at 1 s, 2 s, 4 s; with full jitter over 0 to 8 s it is about 125k/s.
fun backoffMs(attempt: Int): Long {
    val exp = minOf(30_000L, 1_000L shl minOf(attempt, 5))
    return (0..exp).random()   // full jitter
}
client: ping/25s -> no pong -> close -> wait random backoff -> connect(last_seq)
server: replay seq > last_seq from buffer, else send RESYNC

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Relying on TCP to report death.
  • Fixed-interval retry, no jitter.
  • Reconnect without resume (loss) or resume without dedupe (duplicates).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Heartbeat interval vs battery? -> 25 to 30 s foreground; background drops the socket and uses push.
  2. Where do replayed messages come from? -> A short per-user buffer or the message store by sequence.
  3. What if sequence numbers reset on a node failover? -> Make sequences per conversation or per user, stored durably, not per connection.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "retry on close". Senior: heartbeat below NAT timeouts, jitter math, resume plus dedupe, token refresh, REST fallback.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Mobile carriers drop idle NAT mappings after 30 to 60 s; a 120 s heartbeat produced "connected but dead" users until it was shortened.

questions.contextHtml:
A gateway node with 100k connections crashes at 20:00. The remaining 19 nodes hold 1.9M connections. Within 30 s:

connect rate:        200/s -> 38,000/s
gateway CPU:         30% -> 98% (TLS handshakes)
auth DB QPS:         500 -> 41,000, p99 2.3 s
connection count:    sawtooth, nodes dropping 20-60k then re-adding
client log:          reconnect attempt=1 delay=1000 ... attempt=2 delay=2000 (no jitter)

Total connections trending down, not up.
questions.promptHtml: Stabilize the system and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale out the gateways." New nodes join the same storm.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the auth check hit a DB per connect? Are tokens JWT? Is there admission control on connections? Do clients use TLS session resumption?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap accept rate per node (for example 2,000/s), return "retry later" with a jittered delay, temporarily disable the DB auth check in favor of local JWT validation, add auth DB read cache.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Synchronized backoff without jitter; per-connect DB auth; TLS CPU; cascading node failures from overload (sawtooth).
  4. How I'd verify: Handshake rate vs CPU, auth DB query log, client attempt-time distribution.
  5. Root cause: A crash converts 100k clients into a synchronized wave. Handshake plus DB auth makes each connect expensive, overload kills more nodes, which creates more reconnects: positive feedback.
  6. Fix: Short term: admission control and server-sent "reconnect after random(0,60s)". Long term: full jitter, JWT validated locally, TLS session tickets, a connection-rate limit per node, capacity headroom so N-1 failure is absorbed (30%), drain on deploys.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test: kill a node, watch reconnect rate; alert on handshake rate and auth DB QPS.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Local JWT validation means revocation lags until expiry (keep short TTL or a revocation list). Do not just autoscale; it adds cold nodes into the storm.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users cannot get in for minutes; acceptable? -> Prioritize by queueing with jitter; users with active sessions resume first.
  • Region failure? -> Spread the reconnect over time and regions; pre-warm capacity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rolling deploy restarted nodes too fast; each restart pushed clients to peers, and the cascade took 30 minutes to settle until reconnect rate was capped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add nodes.
  • Hire: Jitter, admission control, local auth.
  • Strong hire: Positive-feedback explanation, session tickets, N-1 headroom, chaos test.

questions.contextHtml: A news app has 10M installs. A breaking-news push must reach users within 2 minutes. The current job loops over device tokens with one FCM HTTP call per token from a single worker at 800 sends/s. It takes 3.5 hours. Logs show 8% of calls return UNREGISTERED/NOT_FOUND, and during the last campaign some calls returned 429/503. Delivery receipts show many users got it after the 40-minute mark.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run it in a thread pool." No queue, no token hygiene, no quota awareness.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the content the same for everyone (topics) or personalized? What is our FCM quota? Is collapse_key/TTL set? How fresh must it be (stale news is worthless)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Send via topic ("news-india-breaking") for the shared alert, so FCM does the fan-out instead of per-token calls.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A single sequential worker is the bottleneck (10M / 800 = 12,500 s = 3.5 h); stale tokens waste calls; no backoff on 429.
  4. How I'd verify: Send rate, error breakdown by code, queue age.
  5. Root cause: Serial per-token delivery.
  6. Fix: Topics for broadcasts; for personalized sends, queue (Kafka or SQS), 50 workers at 2,000 sends/s = 100k/s, so 10M in 100 s. Delete tokens on UNREGISTERED; honor Retry-After with backoff plus jitter on 429/503; set ttl of 2 hours and a collapse_key so stale alerts are replaced; high priority for breaking news; payload under about 4 KB with an id, and the app fetches details over HTTPS. Push is a wake-up; REST is the source of truth. Check FCM quota in the docs (verify).
  7. Prevention: Token last-seen cleanup, delivery metrics, send-time SLO alert.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No secrets in payloads. Not rely on push for critical data; users with notifications off or Doze-delayed devices will see it later.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• OEM kills background apps (some Android vendors)? -> Educate users, use high priority, and sync on next open.
  • Personalization per user? -> Segment topics or per-token batches with a queue.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Purging stale tokens shrank a campaign list by 9% and cut error noise enough to expose a real auth bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Threads in one process.
  • Hire: Topics, queue and workers, token cleanup.
  • Strong hire: TTL and collapse, backoff, quota awareness, REST truth.

questions.contextHtml:
A chat client reconnects on failure. Users report that after a tunnel they see messages twice, and sometimes a message they sent shows twice to the recipient. Client code:

override fun onFailure(ws: WebSocket, t: Throwable, r: Response?) {
    connect()                                    // immediately
}
override fun onOpen(ws: WebSocket, r: Response) {
    ws.send("""{"type":"sync","since":${lastSeenTime}}""")
    pending.forEach { ws.send(it.json) }         // resend unsent messages
}
override fun onMessage(ws: WebSocket, text: String) {
    ui.add(parse(text)); lastSeenTime = now()
}

Server replays everything newer than since and persists every send it receives. Messages have no ids.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only fixes "retry immediately". Misses the data-model bugs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are server timestamps monotonic? Can two messages share a timestamp? Does the server ack sends?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Client-side dedupe by content hash as a stopgap; ship a hotfix for ids.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lastSeenTime = now() uses the client clock, not the message's server order, so replay overlaps or misses; (b) resent pending messages have no client_msg_id, so a message that actually reached the server before the drop is stored twice; (c) no dedupe of replayed messages in the UI; (d) immediate reconnect with no backoff or jitter; (e) no token refresh.
  4. How I'd verify: Drop the connection mid-send in a test with a proxy; inspect server logs for two inserts of the same text.
  5. Root cause: At-least-once delivery without idempotency: send retry duplicates, replay duplicates.
  6. Fix: Server assigns a monotonically increasing seq per conversation; the client sends client_msg_id, the server dedupes on it and returns an ack with seq; the client resumes with last_seq (not time); the UI dedupes by (conv, seq); unacked messages are resent with the same client_msg_id.
ws.send("""{"type":"send","client_msg_id":"$id","conv":"$c","text":"$t"}""")
ws.send("""{"type":"resume","conv":"$c","last_seq":$lastSeq}""")
  1. Prevention: Fault-injection tests (drop after send, before ack), property test: N sends give N messages.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Exactly-once is not available; use at-least-once plus idempotent receive. Define ids and ordering on day one; it is the one-way door.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Gap too large to replay? -> Server sends RESYNC; client fetches history over REST.
  • Multi-device? -> Per-device cursors, one server seq per conversation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "duplicate message" bug was fixed three times in the client before someone added server-side dedupe on a client id.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only adds backoff.
  • Hire: Message ids, seq-based resume, dedupe.
  • Strong hire: Ack protocol, client clock bug, fault-injection tests.

questions.contextHtml: "Build live cricket scores for our app." No further detail. Peak: 2M concurrent viewers, a score update every ~3 s (about 200 bytes). Some users also post emoji reactions, the app is often in the background, and the CTO wants it live in 4 weeks with a team of 4.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and what do you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "WebSockets, obviously."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Acceptable delay (2 s or 10 s)? Are reactions two-way and must they be live? Background behavior required? Web too? Is a CDN available?
  2. Immediate mitigation (v1 scope): Ship the score as server-to-client only; defer live reactions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One-way, small, identical to all viewers: the best fit is SSE or polling a cacheable endpoint. Reactions can be aggregated and sent in a 1-second batch.
  4. How I'd verify: Egress math: 2M x 67 B/s = 134 MB/s (about 1.07 Gbps) for SSE; short polling every 3 s on a CDN-cached JSON gives about 667k req/s but the CDN absorbs them.
  5. Root cause of the decision: Direction and fan-out, not interactivity, drive the choice.
  6. Fix (design): Foreground: SSE (or CDN-cached short poll) fed from a pub-sub to edge nodes with ids and Last-Event-ID; about 20 nodes at 100k connections. Background: FCM for key events (wicket, result) using topics with collapse_key. REST endpoint as source of truth after any gap. Reactions: client POST, server aggregates counts and sends them in the stream every second.
Scorer -> pub-sub -> edge SSE nodes -> app (foreground)
Scorer -> FCM topic -> app (background)  ;  app -> REST on gap
  1. Prevention: Load test to 2M connections, reconnect jitter, replay buffer, "stale data" indicator.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not WebSocket for v1: more to build (reconnect, replay) for a one-way feed. Moving to WebSocket later is a two-way door if REST sync and message ids exist; the id and ordering model is the one-way part.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A viral match doubles to 4M? -> Cache-friendly poll fallback and more edge nodes; reduce update size.
  • Reactions need to be instant? -> Then WebSocket for that surface only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A live-score feature built on CDN-cached polling survived a 10x spike where the WebSocket layer of a sister product needed emergency capacity.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks WebSocket without questions.
  • Hire: Asks direction and latency, chooses SSE or cacheable polling plus push.
  • Strong hire: Egress math, fallback, defers reactions, explains reversibility.
